questions.q: What is the ITIL 4 purpose of the service level management practice?
options: To set clear, business-based targets for service levels, and ensure delivery is properly assessed, monitored, and managed against those targets
To handle predefined, user-initiated requests for access or equipment
To restore normal service operation as quickly as possible after an incident
To maintain and improve the effective use of information and knowledge across the organization
questions.explain: Service level management is about setting business-based targets and then actually monitoring and managing delivery against them, not just signing an agreement.

questions.q: What is the key difference between an SLA and an OLA?
options: An SLA is internal to the provider, while an OLA is the customer-facing agreement
An SLA is the agreement between provider and customer; an OLA is an internal agreement between teams that must cooperate to meet the SLA
An OLA always takes priority over the SLA when the two conflict
There is no real difference; the terms are interchangeable in ITIL 4
questions.explain: The SLA is the business-facing promise to the customer; OLAs are the internal agreements between teams that make hitting that promise possible.

questions.q: Where does an underpinning contract fit into service level management?
options: It is the same thing as an SLA, just under a different name
It is an internal agreement between two teams within the same provider organization
It is an external contract with a third-party supplier whose performance feeds into the provider's ability to meet the SLA
It only applies to service requests, never to service levels
questions.explain: An underpinning contract is external, with a supplier such as an internet provider or SaaS vendor, and its performance underpins whether the SLA can be met at all.

questions.q: Why does ITIL 4 push toward output-based SLAs instead of purely technical, component-based metrics?
options: Because component metrics like server uptime or network latency are no longer useful at all
Because output-based SLAs eliminate the need for any technical monitoring
Because customers are not able to understand component-based metrics
Because a component metric like server uptime can look fine while the business still experiences the service as broken, so targets should reflect the outcome the business actually experiences
questions.explain: A server can hit 99.9% uptime while a slow network link or broken integration still makes the service unusable to the business — output-based targets capture what the business actually experiences.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what happens after an SLA is signed?
options: The practice's work is essentially finished once the agreement is signed
Service level management continues with ongoing performance monitoring, regular service review meetings, and renegotiation when targets prove unrealistic
The SLA becomes permanently fixed and can never be renegotiated
Monitoring responsibility shifts entirely to the customer, not the provider
questions.explain: Signing the SLA is the starting point; the ongoing work is monitoring actual performance, reviewing it with the customer, and adjusting targets as needed.
